# Lipid profile dysregulation predicts alcohol withdrawal symptom severity in individuals with alcohol use disorder

**Authors:** Daniel B. Rosoff; Katrin Charlet; Jeesun Jung; Jisoo Lee; Christine Muench; Audrey Luo; Martha Longley; Falk W. Lohoff

**Affiliations:** Section on Clinical Genomics and Experimental Therapeutics, National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, United States

## Abstract

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) is a serious medical condition of high variability in alcohol use disorder (AUD) after drinking cessation. Identification of clinical biomarkers capable of detecting severe AWS is needed. While alcohol consumption and withdrawal are linked with lipid profile dysregulation, the relationship between lipid levels (high-density lipoprotein cholesterol [HDL-C], low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C], and triglycerides) and AWS is unknown. Therefore, this study investigated whether HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides conferred risk for moderate-to-severe AWS symptoms in treatment-seeking individuals (n = 732) admitted to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) alcohol treatment program. Lipid levels were measured upon admission, and the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, Revised (CIWA-Ar) assessed AWS severity for generating a three-level AWS typology (none-to-mild, moderate, and severe). Multivariable multinomial logistic regression examined whether lipid levels were associated with risk for moderate-to-severe AWS. We found significant predictive relationships between AWS and HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides. While extremely high HDL-C (≥100 mg/dL) conferred the highest odds for moderate (4.405, 95% CI, 2.572–7.546, p < 0.001) and severe AWS (5.494, 95% CI, 3.541–8.523, p < 0.001), the lowest odds ratios for moderate AWS (0.493, 95% CI, 0.248–0.981, p = 0.044) and severe AWS (0.303, 95% CI, 0.223–0.411, p < 0.001) were associated with high LDL-C (≥160 mg/dL). The present study demonstrates that altered lipid levels, measured upon admission for inpatient AUD treatment, may help to predict which individuals are at risk for medically relevant moderate-to-severe AWS. This suggests that further research into the role of lipid biomarkers in AWS may be beneficial for identifying biologically determined risk profiles in AUD.

## Introduction

Alcohol use disorder (AUD), estimated to affect approximately 32 million Americans (Grant et al., 2017), is associated with many medical comorbidities (Rehm & Hingson, 2013) and accounts for 10–30% of hospital intensive care unit (ICU) admissions (de Wit, Jones, Sessler, Zilberberg, & Weaver, 2010). Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) is experienced by approximately half of those with AUD who abruptly reduce or completely stop regular alcohol intake (Schuckit, 2014). AWS, with its severe life-threatening form of delirium tremens (DT), is a serious constellation of physical and psychological symptoms, including, among others, anxiety, agitation, tremors, sweating, hyperreflexia, tachycardia, fever, insomnia, nausea, confusion or hallucinations, and seizures (Kattimani & Bharadwaj, 2013) due to central nervous system (CNS) hyperactivity (Dutta et al., 2016). Drinking behavior and history, alcohol withdrawal, past episodes of DT or AWS, as well as elevated levels of alcohol immediately preceding AWS, are identified risk factors for developing a severe AWS (Lechtenberg & Worner, 1992). However, the incidence and severity of withdrawal vary significantly, which necessitates continuous monitoring and assessment during the first hours and days after alcohol cessation to guide appropriate pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments (Schuckit, 2014). Therefore, early identification of patients at increased risk for developing AWS is essential for efficacious treatment (Jesse et al., 2017).

Given the complexity of AWS, attempts have been made to identify biological variables – either direct or indirect markers of alcohol consumption – that are easily measurable in a clinical setting, to aid prediction, monitoring, and assessment for individuals at risk of developing moderate-to-severe AWS (Jesse et al., 2017). The association between chronic alcohol consumption and cholesterol and triglyceride metabolism is well documented (Steiner & Lang, 2017). Heavy alcohol consumption has been shown to contribute to hepatic steatosis (Donohue, 2007; Rosoff, Smith, Mehta, Clarke, & Lohoff, 2019), and is associated with hypertriglyceridemia, possibly from increased chylomicron and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) levels (Chait, Mancini, February, & Lewis, 1972). The most robust alcohol–lipid association is between alcohol consumption and increased high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels (for review, see Charlet & Heinz, 2017; Rosoff, Charlet, et al., 2019). Hirata et al. (2018) recently found that alcohol consumption increases the risk for extremely high HDL-C (>100 mg/dL), which has been linked with increased cardiovascular and all-cause mortality risk, suggesting a U-shaped relationship between HDL-C and disease risk (Hirata et al., 2018; Madsen, Varbo, & Nordestgaard, 2017). However, these studies do not show whether HDL-C levels >100 mg/dL are associated with AWS. Furthermore, animal studies indicate that there may be a mechanistic, dose-dependent link between ethanol consumption and cholesterol metabolism through altered expression of alcohol-activating hepatic sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP-2; a transcription factor involved in coordinating gene expressions of cholesterol-synthesizing enzymes), and the SREBP-2 induced hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) reductase (the rate-limiting key enzyme for cholesterol synthesis) (Justice et al., 2019; Klein et al., 2014; Wang, Yao, & Song, 2010; Yin et al., 2009). Notably, cessation or reduction of alcohol consumption (which has been shown to be associated with reductions of HDL-C levels, changes in HDL-C particle size, and subfraction distribution) also impacts low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride levels (Charlet & Heinz, 2017). In sum, circulating lipid levels may provide additional clinical biomarkers useful for the identification of AWS severity.

Therefore, the aims of this study were to 1) evaluate the association between circulating HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides, measured at the time of participants’ admission to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) inpatient treatment program, and AWS severity, as indicated by the score on the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, Revised (CIWA-Ar) (Sullivan, Sykora, Schneiderman, Naranjo, & Sellers, 1989), and 2) assess whether clinical HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglyceride levels, including extremely high HDL-C, predicted development of subsequent moderate AWS (as indicated by maximum CIWA-Ar scores 8–15) and severe AWS (as indicated by maximum CIWA-Ar scores >15) (Perry, 2014).

## Methods

### Data source

The study included 732 participants recruited at the NIAAA alcohol treatment program, where they were voluntarily admitted to the NIAAA inpatient unit in the NIH Clinical Center between February 2006 and October 2017. All participants met criteria for alcohol dependence (AD) based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th Edition, Text Revision (DSM-IV-TR), as assessed by the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV-TR Axis I Disorders (First, Spitzer, Gibbon, & Williams, 2002). Further, study inclusion criteria were being between 21 and 65 years of age, being literate in English, and not suffering from either active psychotic symptoms or severe cognitive impairment. Following admission, participants were detoxified from alcohol and participated in the alcohol treatment program. For all participants, written informed consent was obtained in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and as approved by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism Review Board, after which participants underwent extensive clinical and physical examinations.

## Assessments

### Alcohol withdrawal severity and inpatient treatment

As part of the standard procedure, the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, Revised (CIWA-Ar), was used in all inpatients upon admission and every 8 h up to day 6 after admission to assess and monitor maximum alcohol withdrawal through the early period of abstinence, and thus evaluate withdrawal intensity. The CIWA-Ar is a 10-item observer-rated scale (Sullivan et al., 1989), with demonstrated inter-rater reliability and validity (Shaw, Kolesar, Sellers, Kaplan, & Sandor, 1981; Sullivan et al., 1989), utilized to guide pharmacological and non-pharmacological management for alcohol withdrawal in a variety of clinical settings (Salottolo, McGuire, Mains, van Doorn, & Bar-Or, 2017). “Mild” withdrawal is indicated by CIWA-Ar scores less than 8; “moderate” withdrawal is indicated by CIWA-Ar scores 8–15, inclusive; and severe withdrawal is indicated by scores >15 (Young, Rores, Murphy, & Dailey, 1987). For purposes of this study, a three-level CIWA-Ar typology was generated according to the clinical thresholds.

Pharmacological inpatient treatment included only benzodiazepines (BZDs; diazepam, oxazepam, or lorazepam), administered based on AWS severity and clinical judgment including prior AWS history. Pharmacological treatment is considered to be “not necessary” for inpatients with CIWA-Ar scores <8; treatment “may be appropriate” for inpatients with scores between 8 and 15, inclusive; and treatment is “strongly indicated” for inpatients with scores >15, scores that have been shown to predict subsequent seizures and DTs requiring emergency treatment (Allan & Harris, 1987). In the current study, 20.1% of inpatients with maximum CIWA-Ar score <8 were treated, compared to 82.3% with maximum CIWA-Ar score 8–15, and 97% with maximum CIWA-Ar >15.

### Self-reported recent alcohol consumption

Information on participants’ past alcohol intake – average number of alcoholic drinks per day, number of heavy drinking days (i.e., 5 or more drinks per day) and total number of drinks in the 90 days prior to admission (TLFB total drinks 90 d) – was assessed using the self-report, Timeline Follow Back (TLFB) (Sobell & Sobell, 1992). Here, a “standard drink” was defined as any alcoholic drink containing 14 g of pure alcohol, which equates the amount of pure alcohol found in one 12-oz. beer (5% alcohol), one 5-oz. glass of wine (12% alcohol), or one 1.5-oz. glass of distilled spirits (40% alcohol) (NIAAA, 1999).

### Blood collection and assays

Samples were collected upon admission to the NIAAA treatment center and processed by the NIH Clinical Center Department of Laboratory Medicine. Blood and plasma samples were obtained using standard methods. Plasma samples were obtained from three IRB-approved protocols. Participants were nil per os (NPO [nothing by mouth]) for approximately 10 h prior to blood collection, and after overnight bed rest, all bloods were drawn at approximately 0800 h. LDL-C, HDL-C, total cholesterol, and triglycerides were measured using standard procedures in mg/dL. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alkaline phosphatase were measured using standard procedures in U/L. LDL-C, HDL-C, and triglycerides typologies were generated, with cutoff points based on values used in the ATP-III guideline (National Cholesterol Education Program, 2001), but we added HDL-C 60–99 mg/dL, and ≥100 mg/dL to more closely examine the relationship between extremely high HDL-C and AWS.

## Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics were computed comparing the CIWA-Ar AWS categories with respect to the distributions of lipids (levels and groups), as well as socio-demographics, past alcohol consumption, liver function (LFT) levels, BZD administration and dosage, and statin administration and dosage. While measures of interest (maximum CIWA-Ar score; HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglyceride levels [mg/dL]; LFT levels) were proven by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test to be non-normally distributed, according distribution appropriate tests were performed to differentiate across and between groups, e.g., Kruskall-Wallace (non-normal continuous), chi-squared (categorical), or exact Fisher test when expected cell frequencies were <5 (categorical). p values were corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. The trend in p value was computed using the Spearman test. Additionally, Spearman rank-based correlation coefficients and p values for continuous variable distributions (including, but not limited to, maximum CIWA-Ar score, not groups; HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglyceride levels [mg/dL], not groups; and LFT levels) were also computed. Descriptive statistics and correlations were computed using the compareGroups and Hmisc packages, respectively, in the R environment for statistical computing and visualization.

### Multivariable regression modeling

Multivariable multinomial logistics regression was used to estimate the parameters of the underlying logistics model of the CIWA-Ar three-category typology (wherein the log odds of the value “1” for any of the three categories is a linear combination of the predictors/covariates), and to obtain (from those estimated parameters) the relative risk ratios (odds ratios) for the lipids typologies predictors, controlling for other lipids typologies, liver function test (LFT) levels, and TLFB total drinks (90 days prior), and controlling for clinical treatment (BZD administration) in alternative models. All lipids typologies were considered simultaneously – not one at a time – to obviate omitted variable bias (OVB), given the observed mild to moderate inter-correlations (Table 2). Given the prior literature linking alcohol consumption to subsequent AWS, referenced herein, TLFB total drinks (90 days prior) was included as a potential confounder to determine the effect of the lipid typologies on CIWA-Ar independently of the effect of TLFB total drinks on CIWA-Ar. BZD was similarly included as a potential confounder, given that BZD was administered based on threshold CIWA-Ar clinically assessed during treatment, as well as on past history of DTs and past AWS. The Hosmer–Lemeshow (HL) test for goodness of fit was used for the multinomial logistic regressions, comparing observed with expected outcome frequencies, and computing a chi-squared test statistic: a non-significant HL p value signifies no evidence that the observed and expected frequencies differ, and thus, signifies good model fit. Finally, exploratory multivariable models were estimated using binomial logistic regression of BZD administration to obtain relative risk ratios (odds) for the lipids typologies, controlling for other lipids typologies, and liver function test (LFT) levels. All regression models were also controlled for socio-demographic covariates: age at admission to the NIAAA program, gender, education, race, and body mass index (BMI). For these analyses (except where indicated otherwise), significance was evaluated using 0.05 level two-sided tests. Multinomial log-linear regression analyses were carried out using the nnet (neural networks) package, and binomial regressions, using the stats package, both in the R environment for statistical computing and visualization (R Development Core Team 2018).

## Results

### Descriptive statistics and correlations among phenotypes

CIWA-Ar AWS groups are distributed in the full sample of 732 treatment-seeking adults (assessed AUD) as follows: mild AWS, 59.7%; moderate AWS, 27.0%; and severe AWS, 13.3% (Table 1). The distributions of HDL-C levels (but neither LDL-C nor triglycerides), as well as gender, alcohol consumption behavior, LFTs, and BZD dosing, differed significantly between the CIWA-Ar AWS groups (p < 0.001) (Table 1). Further, only 21 out of 732 patients were pharmacologically treated with statins during the inpatient program with no differences detected between the CIWA-Ar AWS groups regarding statin administration or average dosage (Table 1). Unadjusted correlation analysis showed HDL-C significantly positively correlated with maximum CIWA-Ar score (ρ = 0.275, p < 0.001). LDL-C significantly negatively correlated with maximum CIWA-Ar score (ρ = −0.139, p < 0.001), but triglycerides were not significantly correlated (ρ = −0.139, p < 0.001) (Table 2, Fig. 1). Further unadjusted correlational analyses tested the same associations, but separately in males and females. We found similar associations in both groups: positive associated HDL-C with maximum CIWA-Ar score (males: ρ = 0.244, p < 0.001; females: ρ = 0.242, p ≤ 0.001), negative associated LDL-C with maximum CIWA-Ar score (males: ρ = −0.197, p = 0.004; females: ρ = −0.098, p = 0.027), but triglycerides were not significantly associated with CIWA-Ar score (males: ρ = −0.047, p = 0.492; females: ρ = −0.045, p = 0.306) (Fig. 2). Multivariable multinomial logistics analyses, following hereto, categorize HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides according to clinical thresholds, to elucidate these descriptive statistics and correlations.

## Multivariable regression modeling

We found significant predictive relationships between the CIWA-Ar AWS typology and both HDL-C and LDL-C typologies, in the expected opposite directions, controlling for LFTs, BMI, and TLFB total drinks 90 d (Table 3, model 1; HL p = 0.225, signifying good model fit). Here, HDL-C, i.e., level III ([60,100] mg/dL) raised significantly the odds for moderate and severe CIWA-Ar AWS, compared to the reference, mild CIWA-Ar group (moderate AWS: OR, 2.496, 95% CI, 1.628–3.828, p < 0.001; severe AWS: OR, 2.621, 95% CI, 1.777–3.866, p < 0.001). Further, extremely high HDL-C, i.e., level IV (≥100 mg/dL), was associated with even higher odds for moderate and severe CIWA-Ar (moderate AWS: OR, 4.405, 95% CI, 2.572–7.546, p < 0.001; severe AWS: OR, 5.494, 95% CI, 3.541–8.523, p < 0.001) (Table 3, model I).

In contrast, borderline high LDL-C [level III (130,160 mg dL)] was associated with significantly lower odds for moderate and severe CIWA-Ar AWS, compared to the reference mild CIWA-Ar AWS (moderate AWS: OR, 0.503, 95% CI, 0.280–0.904, p = 0.022; severe AWS: OR, 0.425, 95% CI, 0.200–0.903, p = 0.026). High LDL-C [level IV (≥160 mg/dL)] lowered further the odds for moderate and severe CIWA-Ar AWS (moderate AWS: OR, 0.493, 95% CI, 0.248–0.981, p = 0.044; severe AWS: OR, 0.303, 95% CI, 0.223–0.411, p < 0.001) (Table 3, model I).

We also found significant predictive relationships between moderate CIWA-Ar AWS and triglycerides. Similarly to HDL-C, borderline high triglycerides [level II ([150,200 mg/dL)] conferred significantly higher odds for moderate CIWA-Ar AWS (OR, 1.729, 95% CI, 1.000–2.991, p = 0.050). High triglycerides [level III (≥200 mg/dL)] predicted even higher odds for moderate CIWA-Ar AWS (OR, 2.434, 95% CI, 1.393–4.255, p = 0.002).

Controlling for BZD administration, we still found significant but attenuated predictive relationships (Table 3, model II; HL p = 0.876, signifying good model fit). We observed, however, in preliminary multivariable logistics analysis, significant predictive relationships between BZD (the dichotomous outcome) and HDL-C levels III and IV (positive), and LDL-C levels II and IV (negative), even controlling for initial CIWA-Ar AWS (Table 3, models I and II), suggesting that BZD moderates the associations between both HDL-C and LDL-C and CIWA-Ar AWS.

## Discussion

The present study investigated the relationship between plasma HDL-C, LDL-C, triglycerides, and AWS severity in a sample of patients undergoing treatment for AUD. Our study demonstrates that extremely high HDL-C levels significantly increased the odds of developing moderate and severe AWS. We also found that elevated LDL-C reduced the risk for moderate and severe AWS, while high triglyceride levels increased the risk for moderate AWS.

These findings extend existing research demonstrating that abrupt cessation of alcohol consumption is associated with changes in cholesterol levels (Charlet & Heinz, 2017), and may also have clinical implications. Here, HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglyceride levels may be useful clinical predictors of AWS severity, which add to the growing list of biomarkers, including elevated heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and temperature, as well as mean corpuscular volume (Findley et al., 2010) and liver function enzymes (Kattimani & Bharadwaj, 2013; Perry, 2014). These biomarkers are readily available in clinical settings and are therefore useful in predicting AWS (Jesse et al., 2017). In particular, clinicians should be aware of possible increased moderate or severe AWS among individuals abstaining from alcohol consumption presenting with extremely high HDL-C, which has already been shown to be associated with an increased cardiovascular and all-cause mortality risk (Madsen et al., 2017). While increased HDL-C levels are generally considered to have an apparent protective effect regarding cardiovascular diseases (De Oliveira E Silva et al., 2000), HDL-C physiology with its subfractions is complex and not yet fully understood. Thus, it could be speculated that increased disease risk among those with extremely high HDL-C may be due to variation in HDL-C particle composition (Madsen et al., 2017). Further, recent studies even seem to contradict previous (epidemiologic) observations of a beneficiary association between higher HDL-C levels and reduced CVD risk (e.g., Barter et al., 2007; Lincoff et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2012). Pharmacologic interventions aimed at enhancing cellular cholesterol efflux capacity with drugs like the cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitors evacetrapib (Lincoff et al., 2017), torcetrapib (Barter et al., 2007), or dalcetrapib (Schwartz et al., 2012) did significantly increase HDL-C levels as expected but – surprisingly – did not yield in reduced stroke, CVD, or coronary heart disease risk. Therefore, the association between lipids, and HDL-C in particular, needs to be further investigated considering that there is a rather U-shaped relationship between HDL-C and disease risk (Hirata et al., 2018; Madsen et al., 2017). Additionally, chronic heavy alcohol consumption or AUD may impair HDL-C normal functioning via increasing inflammation, which affects negatively both quantity and composition of HDL particles (e.g., loss of anti-inflammatory and antioxidative proteins while gaining proinflammatory proteins), resulting in impaired antiatherogenic effects (e.g., Rosenson et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2009). Of note, as lipids may act as indirect biomarkers of alcohol consumption (Rosoff, Charlet, et al., 2019), our results persisted even after controlling for recent alcohol consumption, indicating a potential mechanism of action beyond current alcohol-induced changes.

It is likely that other molecular targets in the lipid-regulating pathways are affected by alcohol as well, such as proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin 9 (PCSK9) (Lee et al., 2019; Lohoff, 2018; Lohoff et al., 2018), with indirect effects on HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides. Further, a recent preclinical study found that the ketogenic diet (KD), a diet high in fat and low in carbohydrates that modulates plasma cholesterol and triglyceride levels (Paoli, Rubini, Volek, & Grimaldi, 2013), was linked to reduced AWS tremors in alcohol-dependent rats (Dencker et al., 2018). However, that contrary indication may be due, in part, to the diet’s impact on cholesterol homeostasis. The KD diet has been described to confer neuroprotection via anti-inflammatory processes and prevention of glutamate-induced neural apoptosis and necrosis reflected in the KD-related anticonvulsant effects and the observed reduced neuronal excitability, partially due to beneficiary changes in blood lipid profiles (Gasior, Rogawski, & Hartman, 2006; Paoli et al., 2013). Further, caloric restriction has been reported to promote cleansing metabolic effects by activating autophagy and lipophagy in liver, brain, fat, and muscle tissue (Martinez-Lopez et al., 2017; Singh & Cuervo, 2012). Therefore, without beneficiary caloric restriction, dysfunctional HDL-C as seen in AUD (Rosenson et al., 2016; Yin et al., 2009) may remain and accumulate in the metabolic system of AUD patients together with detrimental changes in cholesterol homeostasis. Here, disturbances in brain cholesterol metabolism were shown to be associated with structural and functional deficits in neurons, which may act as an underlying mechanism that facilitates hyperexcitability and increased risk for AWS symptoms like seizures in AUD patients (Karasinska et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2009). Thus, the ongoing Clinical Trial investigating the effect of KD on AWS in AUD patients (NIAAA, 2017) might elucidate this relationship and open new avenues of treatment options for patients at risk for severe AWS and extremely high HDL-C levels.

Interestingly, we further observed that patients with borderline high and high LDL-C levels showed 50–70% lowered odds for experiencing moderate/severe AWS symptomatology compared to mild AWS severity. Here, recent study results derived from a large male cohort of 21,572 subjects showed different sensitivities of both LDL-C and HDL-C to subjects’ habitual alcohol consumption, indicating independent effects of both lipids on health outcomes such as CVD (Wakabayashi, 2018). However, whether extremely high HDL-C or high LDL-C and concurrent alteration in HDL-C/LDL-C physiology may directly result from chronic heavy alcohol consumption, and therefore might be considered as clinical biomarkers of recent heavy drinking and consecutive withdrawal remains to be investigated in future studies. Again, in the present study the results persisted even after controlling for alcohol consumption.

Similarly, controlling for benzodiazepine dosage attenuated the conferred risk by lipids, but significance remained, suggesting lipids may be robust markers of AWS. Additional multivariable logistic analyses showed significant predictive relationships between BZD and HDL-C and LDL-C (Table 3), suggesting that BZD may moderate the relationships between HDL-C and LDL-C with AWS.

## Limitations

Potential limitations of our study should be addressed. First, this study investigated AWS severity in total as a complex clinical phenomenon including and not separating all AWS subcomponents. Thus, future studies are warranted to explore in more detail associations between lipid dysregulations and specific AWS subcomponents, such as vegetative versus anxiety/mood-related symptoms. Moreover, information regarding lifetime drinking history, last drink/heavy drinking prior to blood collection, or history of AWS were not included with this study, which may influence CIWA-Ar scores (Becker, 2008) or lipid profiles (Charlet & Heinz, 2017). Metabolic normalization including HDL-C and triglycerides has been reported for short-term alcohol reduction or total abstinence of 3–14 weeks in previous studies (cf. Charlet & Heinz, 2017). Thus, future studies like RCTs should consider enrolling patients within the same abstinence time frame and/or control for the abstinent days. Being cross-sectional, the present study was unable to assess the causality of the associations between lipid levels and AWS. AWS is a complex phenotype; it is likely that multiple factors contribute to its etiology, including genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors (Dutta et al., 2016; Tawa, Hall, & Lohoff, 2016). In addition, there are likely several intercorrelations between various phenotypes related to AUD, including correlations between drinking severity, HDL changes, CIWA severity, and BDZ use. Furthermore, repeated episodes of alcohol withdrawal were speculated to be a risk factor predicting increased severity of subsequent withdrawals by activating a kindling process of CNS hyperirritability (Ballenger & Post, 1978; Brown, Anton, Malcolm, & Ballenger, 1988). Moreover, genetic variants of the Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) genotype were found to contribute either to an increased (ApoE3) or decreased (ApoE2) risk of experienced withdrawal seizures (Wilhelm et al., 2007). ApoE polymorphism is among many other functions involved in initiation of HDL biogenesis, with ApoE3 being herein more effective than ApoE4 (Marais, 2019). Therefore, genetic variation, e.g., in the apolipoprotein ApoE polymorphisms, may further modulate the observed association between HDL-C level (and other lipids) and AWS. Again, early studies showed that although BZD treatment alleviates acute AWS, BZD treatment seems to have no effect on the kindling process and the accompanied increased likelihood of future withdrawal seizures (Brown et al., 1988). Since our study design only allowed to control for the dichotomous variable of BZD treatment, future studies with different study designs may also include a detailed history of previous alcohol withdrawals, other variables of (more detailed) drinking history, and benzodiazepine history. Given the known changes in lipid levels during abstinence (Charlet & Heinz, 2017), future work investigating these longitudinal alterations may clarify the mechanisms of these associations and could help to provide important information for identifying individuals at risk for medically relevant AWS conditions and monitoring AWS per se. Future studies could also investigate other predictors for severe complications of AWS, such as seizures and/or delirium tremens. Second, the extent to which these findings apply to different alcohol treatment settings is unclear. Non-emergency patients admitted to the NIAAA treatment centers may differ substantially from the clinical presentation in emergency settings (Jesse et al., 2017), and replication studies in other settings like emergency care may enhance our understanding. Finally, lipid levels, like other indirect biomarkers of alcohol withdrawal, are influenced by many disease states, which may impact sensitivity and specificity related to predicting AWS (Jesse et al., 2017). Future studies might therefore consider inclusion of elaborate hepatic or metabolic assessments to help in differentiating or identifying influences of diverse disease states on AWS severity.

## Conclusion

The present study demonstrates that altered lipid levels, measured upon admission for inpatient AUD treatment, predict subsequent moderate and severe AWS. These easily obtainable, routine lipid panels may be used by clinicians in the future when clinically relevant AWS is suspected. Despite limitations, these findings suggest that further research into the role of lipid biomarkers in AWS may be beneficial for identifying biologically determined risk profiles in AUD, and highlight the need for additional investigation of clinical outcomes associated with extremely high HDL-C.
